previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: The patient was admitted with chest pain and found to be in alcohol withdrawal, with new-onset atrial fibrillation and suspected untreated pneumonia. He had a history of coronary artery disease with stents, heart failure, and polysubstance abuse. Labs and imaging ruled out acute myocardial infarction, but an echocardiogram showed reduced ejection fraction at 25–30%. He was treated with benzodiazepines for withdrawal, antibiotics for pneumonia, and restarted on aspirin and lisinopril. Despite counseling on the risks, he chose to leave against medical advice. He was discharged with a prescription for levofloxacin and instructions to follow up with his primary care provider for ongoing management of heart failure, atrial fibrillation, and substance use.

Brief Hospital Course:
Mr. ___ is a ___ y/o male with a history of alcohol abuse, CAD 
s/p PCI to OM2, RCA and L circ in ___ and ___, DES to RCA, 
HLD, obesity, COPD, and systolic heart failure with last EF 
___ in ___, who presents with CHF exacerbation, and 
periumbilical abdominal pain, found to have atrial fibrillation 
with RVR.

#CHF exacerbation: The patient has an ejection fraction of 
___ based on ECHO from ___ and a history of medication 
non-adherence. He presented with shortness of breath, elevated 
JVP, lower extremity edema, and a BNP of 3960. He was treated 
with Lasix 40 mg IV with good urine output and a goal of net -1L 
daily.  His electrolytes were monitored and repleted. 
Unfortunately, he decided to leave AMA on hospital day 3 (see 
AMA note in OMR) . The risks of electrolyte imbalances as well 
as worsening of symptoms were reviewed with the patient. He 
expressed understanding of these risks and still decided to 
leave against medical advice. He was discharged with a 
prescription for furosemide and extensively counseled on the 
importance of follow up with his PCP as soon as possible given 
the risk for electrolyte disturbances and encouraged to limit 
his salt intake to ___ daily.

#Abdominal pain: The etiology of his abdominal pain was still 
unclear at the time the patient left AMA, though suspected to be 
due to abdominal wall strain and ? of hernia based on the 
physical exam. LFTs were normal and lipase was normal. Given the 
patients history of Hepatitis C, he did undergo an abdominal 
ultrasound to assess for HCC, which revealed splenomegaly, 
though no ascites, and a small 3 mm non-obstructing L renal 
stone, which was unlikely to be the cause of his symptoms. 
Unfortunately, the patient left AMA before the ultimate etiology 
of his abdominal pain could be understood.

# Afib with RVR: CHADS2 Score. The patient presented in atrial 
fibrillation with RVR, likely secondary to CHF exacerbation. The 
first note of this was during his ___ hospitalization for 
EtOH detoxification. He was placed on telemetry and treated with 
Diltiazem PRN Afib with ventricular rate >110. He required 
several doses on admission in the ED, but did not require it on 
the floor through the rest of his hospital stay until he left 
AMA on hospital day 3. His home dose of Metoprolol 75 mg BID was 
continued as well as ASA 325. Unfortunately on day 3 he decided 
to leave the hospital AMA. He was strongly encouraged to take 
Aspirin 325 mg daily to reduce his risk of stroke, and expressed 
understanding. Given his history of medication non-adherence and 
episodes of leaving the hospital AMA, he was not started on 
Coumadin. However, he was strongly encouraged to follow up with 
his primary care physician as soon as possible, at which time 
Pradaxa can be an alternative. 

# CAD s/p PCI to OM2, RCA and L circ in ___ and ___, DES to 
RCA 
in ___: Patient admitted on Lopressor 75 mg BID. Though not 
compliant with the statin and lisinopril he was previously 
prescribed. His troponin was negative x2 during this hospital 
admission and asymptomatic.  His Lopressor was continued 
in-house, and he was restarted on Lisinopril. His LDL of 128 is 
above goal given his history of MI. Unfortunately the patient 
left AMA on hospital day 3 before a discussion about starting a 
statin could occur. He was highly encouraged to follow up with 
his primary care physician, where discussion about the need for 
a statin can take place.

# History of polysubstance abuse: Urine and serum toxicology 
were negative. He was given a nicotine patch, and was seen by 
social work who enrolled him in PACT.

# Hx of Hepatitis C: HCV + in ___, but undetectable viral load 
in ___, LFTs normal
and ultrasound revealed splenomegaly, no ascites, and no 
evidence of HCC in the liver.

# Anxiety: Continued clonazepam at home dose

# HLD: Lipid panel was normal, but will likely need a statin in 
the future, as noted above.

Transitional issues:
1. Patient will need monitoring of his electrolytes as he was 
started on lasix during this hospital stay. 
2. Patient with Atrial fibrillation with CHADS 2, currently on 
ASA. Given his history of non-compliance he is not a good 
candidate for coumadin, but might try a trial of Pradaxa.
3. The patient left AMA before a discussion about initiation of 
a statin occurred. His LDL of 128 is above goal given his 
history of MI, and he will need to be started on a statin.
